1:
On the first proverb the commentators agree about the image and differ about its point. Gill and Ellicott both stress how rare untimely weather was in Palestine, where rain during the wheat harvest counted as a marvel and did nothing but obstruct the reapers. Clarke draws the plain inference that nothing here suits its season. Delitzsch and Ellicott then turn from the harm honour does to society toward the harm it does the man: it will only injure him, since he will use it unjustly and reason falsely from it, and it confirms him in the good opinion he already holds of himself, leaving him less willing than before to learn anything. Henry keeps his eye on the commonwealth instead. Preferment for the worthless is common enough, folly being often set in great dignity; and it is as real a disorder in a state as unseasonable weather is in the year, since men lacking the wisdom to discern virtue will use power to discourage it and countenance its opposite.

The causeless curse draws out the ornithology. Gill notes that the Hebrew name of the swallow comes from liberty, since it flies boldly and nests in houses without fear, and that the other bird may be a sparrow or a wild pigeon. Clarke has an undeserved malediction fluttering about the neighbourhood for a season and then vanishing like a migrant, never lighting on the innocent man it was aimed at. Wesley reads the flight as escape from the fowler. Henry finds two lessons: the folly of passion, which scatters anathemas on presumption, mistaking either the person or the fact, and in great men becomes a kind of impotent malice; and the safety of innocence, since such a curse harms its object no more than a bird passing overhead. Ellicott grounds that last point in the text, observing that the Hebrew margin substitutes to him for not, so that the curse comes home to its author — a thought several English proverbs also carry.

At the whip and the bridle Delitzsch reports and rejects an attempt to tidy the verse. Michaelis wished to reverse the implements, giving the bridle to the horse and the whip to the ass; but the pairing is a figure in which each belongs to both, a horse being bridled as well as whipped, and the rhythm of the line accounts for the order. Henry takes the comparison at its harshest: sin has sunk men so far below themselves that they are not to be governed except by force or fear, and the prince who was told in the first verse not to honour a fool is told here to hold him down.

Then comes the pair of sentences that seem to cancel each other, and everyone feels the pressure. Henry calls it the noble security of the scripture style, which appears to contradict itself and does not: never match a boaster with boasting, a railer with railing, or one great lie with another, yet answer when silence would be read as weakness, for a reply fitted to the man is a reply to the point. Delitzsch reads the two occurrences of the phrase in two senses: in the first, to treat the foolish premise as worth entertaining, which levels you with him, since a fool can ask more than ten wise men can answer; in the second, to give folly what it deserves, a short sharp reply that may shame him into self-knowledge. Clarke reaches the same distinction through Warburton, who forbids the defender of religion to imitate the insulter's sophistry, buffoonery and scurrility, while requiring him to confute the fool out of the fool's own principles. Ellicott adds an example rather than an argument: Christ never answered a question that ought not to have been asked, but always put it by. Wesley compresses the whole to two glosses, imitating folly against supplying what folly requires.
6:
Whose legs are cut off when a fool carries the message? Delitzsch says the sender's own, on the idiom by which a man breaks his own neck: he meant to add the messenger's legs to his and has lost the pair he had, and where a faithful errand refreshes, this leaves him swallowing injury. Henry lists what happens — the charge misunderstood, half forgotten, the rest awkwardly delivered — and adds that people judge a master by his messenger. Ellicott and Wesley read the mutilation the other way: he wants the business done and might as well cut the legs off the man he sends, bidding one go who has none. Clarke quotes older English Bibles, which leave the sender halt in his feet and drinking wickedness; Wesley notes that drinking in scripture means receiving in quantity.

The lame man of the next verse is textually harder than he appears. Delitzsch canvasses the attempts: the Greek made the opening word an imperative and took the legs away, the Syriac turned it into a condition — give the lame their walking and you may take wise words from a fool — and later readers softened it to a command to remove what is useless anyway. None satisfies him, a plainer imperative having lain ready had the poet wanted one. Ellicott prefers to let the legs simply hang, useless, since fools can make no more of a proverb than a cripple of his limbs; Gill and Wesley picture the man attempting to dance, his infirmity becoming his exposure. The ninth verse repeats that comparison with a sharper figure, and Delitzsch keeps it dangerous: a saying in such a mouth is a thorn in a drunkard's hand, an instrument that teaches when used properly and here only wounds. He refuses the ancient reading by which the thorn grows there, thorns growing in nobody's hand; Gill observes that the man does not even feel it.

The stone and the sling divide them further. Gill piles up possibilities: a stone fastened so it cannot be discharged, a jewel dropped among rubble heaped over an executed criminal, or an ordinary stone bound in purple, which is merely ridiculous. Clarke follows the versions into stranger country: an old manuscript Bible sends a stone into a heap of money, Coverdale casts a jewel upon the gallows, and the Latin throws one onto a heap sacred to Mercury. Delitzsch defends the traditional sling, the Hebrew noun coming from the verb to sling, and refuses the alternative because the word for what is bound means a grain, not a missile. Ellicott and Wesley find the sense plain either way: the stone leaves the sling and is seen no more, or is tied so it cannot, and honour parts from a fool as quickly.

Delitzsch declares the tenth verse more obscure than anything preceding, revocalizes a word, and renders it so that the reward and the hirer of the fool pass away; he dismisses the Greek as a failed rescue, and notes that the Syriac, splitting one word in two, produces a drunken man sailing over the sea, which means nothing. The English translators left the difficulty visible, printing one reading in the text and another in the margin, and Henry expounds both: the equity of a good God, repaying ignorant folly with few stripes and presumption with many, or the iniquity of a great man who grieves everyone and hires fools and criminals to do it, so that subjects should pray for those in authority. Clarke locates the ambiguity in one word, which may mean the great God or a great man. Ellicott judges the received rendering unsustainable in Hebrew, preferring a contrast between the master who oversees his own work and the fool who hires any passer-by. Wesley alone keeps the plain sense: the recompense deserved will certainly be given, whether the sin was ignorant or wilful.
11:
The dog draws unusual agreement. Gill has the animal sickened by what it ate, casting the load up and returning to lick it from the ground; Delitzsch confirms that dogs do devour their vomit again, and notes that the apostle who later quotes the saying did not take his wording from the Greek. Henry finds two things here. Sin grows hateful even to the sinner, who under a convinced conscience brings it up and appears willing to be rid of it; yet once relieved he returns, having been convinced and never converted. Ellicott presses compulsion rather than choice: the man knows his folly is ruinous, but vice has become second nature and he could not escape if he wished. Clarke contributes only a pointer to the apostle's use of the words.

Self-conceit is treated as the worse condition, and each says why. Delitzsch puts it as a proportion: the sinner who does not imagine himself righteous is likelier to be converted than the self-righteous, and the fool aware of his ignorance likelier to be set right than one who thinks himself wise, the great obstacle being the belief that none is needed. Gill measures the gap between what a man knows of nature, government, morals or God and the opinion he holds of that knowledge, and names the religious form of the disease: righteousness placed in outward observance, imperfection excused by good intention, and in some a fancied perfection, all flowing from ignorance of one's own heart. Henry describes the man from outside — opinionative, dogmatical, censorious, puffed up by what little he knows — and reports Solomon's experience that no pupils were harder to teach than those unaware of needing it. Ellicott illustrates from the gospel, where the strayed came back at the preaching while those who supposed they needed nothing rejected the counsel offered them.

With the sluggard the tone shifts from diagnosis to portraiture. Delitzsch settles the beast — the Hebrew names a lion, not a jackal — and takes the streets of the second clause as rows of houses. Henry catches the evasion: what the man dreads is the road and the marketplace, anywhere work waits; the lion is a difficulty he pleads but has not met, since lions keep their dens by daylight, and it is foolish to be frightened off real duties by imagined ones. On the hinge none can improve the figure. Delitzsch notes that the door swings without ever leaving the narrow arc allowed it, and that the comparison bites because the diligent man goes out through that same door to work while the sluggard revolves on his mattress; the Hebrew name for him means one glued to his place. Gill and Wesley put it in a line: moved, never removed. Henry turns it on religious professors, hung upon the two hinges of world and flesh, treading their round of outward duties like a horse in a mill and no nearer heaven for it.

The hand in the bosom Henry reads as pretence — cold, or lamed, or blistered by yesterday's labour — remarking how common it is for those who will not do a thing to claim they cannot, and calling the failure to lift food to the mouth an elegant hyperbole in which the sin is its own punishment. The closing boast puzzles Delitzsch, who denies any necessary link between laziness and conceit, then supplies the sluggard's reasoning: hard work ruins the health, dulls a man to the pleasures of living, and the cleverest are commonly cracked. Seven he takes as a round number, against a suggestion that it recalls a royal council. Gill calls the idea a contradiction in terms, since a man too slothful to use the means of knowledge cannot be wise; Henry allows that rendering a reason is genuine wisdom, and observes that seven such reasoners might argue with this man all day to no effect.
17:
Delitzsch introduces this run as caricatures recommending peace by showing its opposite, then finds the first syntactically awkward: the two participles stand side by side without a connective, and the sense required is not that a man in a rage happens to walk past, but that walking past he falls into a rage. Ellicott prefers to translate the verb as excited by the quarrel rather than meddling in it. Gill sharpens the offence: the passer-by does not merely interfere but takes a side, and instead of playing peacemaker blows the thing into a larger flame. Henry allows the duty of reconciling others while refusing the role of partisan: a man who would not be hasty in his own quarrel has less business in another's, and to volunteer is to court trouble. His gloss on the dog is the best thing in the group: hold on and your hands are full and you can do nothing else; let go and he flies at you. Clarke observes that the saying holds ninety-nine times in a hundred where the quarrel is domestic, and Wesley reduces it to needless hazard.

The madman and his weapons produce more disagreement than the picture suggests. Delitzsch reports that the participle has no settled rendering, the older translators giving malicious, testing, vainglorious, injurious and a spiritual successor, and that two Jewish commentators went astray by confusing the root with a similar one. Gill lists options too — a man feigning madness to cover his mischief, one who hides so the arrows cannot be traced, one who merely wears himself out — and notes that the cognate Arabic word means to play, which suits the excuse that follows. Ellicott explains the firebrands as arrows carrying blazing material to ignite whatever they struck, and Wesley leaves the last noun as any instrument of death. Henry turns the whole on the excuse. Deceivers think themselves polished and cunning and are lunatics, no madness being greater than deliberate sin; and the plea of sport will not stand, for a man who sins in jest must repent in earnest, truth and a neighbour's reputation being too valuable to sell for a joke, and a false report raised in mirth easily spread in malice. Clarke asks simply how many reputations this kind of sport has killed.

On the talebearer the analysis is mechanical and the moral fierce. Delitzsch distinguishes the two Hebrew words for coal, one black and unlit, the other glowing, and notes what the three terms share: black coal feeds burning coal, wood sustains fire, and the contentious man exists to heat a quarrel — each a means to an end. Gill makes the same point from the half-burnt brand, which takes fire quickly from live coals and becomes like them. Henry treats contention itself as the fire, burning up whatever is good in a family or society, and identifies the fuel: tales are fireballs, and whisperers are incendiaries who ought not to be tolerated, since old grievances die out once nobody brings new ones. Clarke adds what the proverb leaves unsaid, that the listener is as much an agent of discord as the carrier, since slander cannot spread unless somebody receives it — the receiver, as the English saying has it, being as bad as the thief, and hanged accordingly.

The closing line of the group is a repetition, as Gill notes, of a proverb already given and gathered here again by Hezekiah's men. Its meaning divides the commentators sharply. Henry follows the English and reads wounds — deep ones, in the vitals, injuring the reputation of the man spoken against and the charity of the hearer, and past the reach of any later retraction. Delitzsch renders the same clause as dainty morsels that glide down into the innermost parts, which makes the verse a comment on the appetite of the hearer rather than the injury of the absent.
23:
What are burning lips? Wesley alone takes the heat for malice, a tongue on fire with hatred and worth as little as dross that apes silver. The rest hear feigned warmth. Delitzsch identifies the dross as litharge, the lead compound skimmed off in the old refining of silver and still used to glaze earthenware; the figure is a cheap body faced with a costly surface, and he renders the second half as lips glowing with love over a base heart. Clarke pictures a vessel plated with base metal to pass for silver, not even its outside pure; Ellicott calls the glazing a well-known ornament. Gill and Henry admit both readings and prefer the second, Henry noting that malicious words and malicious will pair as naturally as a shard with dross, both fit for the dunghill, while the flattering version imposes on the weak though a wise man sees through it, which is the sense the verses following require.

The next verse turns on a single verb. Delitzsch reports that every ancient translator took it as becoming known, but insists the form equally bears the opposite, to make oneself unrecognisable by a change of clothes or countenance. Gill records the split without resolving it: the hater conceals his grudge until his opportunity comes, or else, on the older versions, he is known by his lips, since watch him long enough and he gives himself away. Henry ignores the question and expounds the concealment, illustrating from two biblical murderers who spoke kindly to their victims first. To lay up deceit is to hold the mischief in store until its victim is caught at a disadvantage: malice with the serpent's subtlety as well as his venom.

Hence the warning against fair speech, which Gill extends beyond flattery to the suppliant and the pitiful tone, bidding the hearer suspect a snake in the grass; Clarke says such professions should go for nothing, and Ellicott takes the seven as a round number. Henry gives the caution both ways — do not be deceived, since even the tempter spoke fair in the garden; and do not deceive, since the disguise cannot hold. On that exposure Delitzsch notes only the rarity of a proverb opening with a future, while Ellicott renders the clause as a concession: hatred may hide behind deceit, but the wickedness will show in open assembly as soon as an occasion for indulging it arrives. Gill offers an alternative in which the hatred lies covered in a desert place, unobserved. Henry supplies the epigram: love is the best armour and the worst cloak.

The pit and the stone need no explaining and get it. Gill and Ellicott recall the hunter's covered pit into which the pursuer sometimes drops; Delitzsch traces the saying to a psalm and into French and Italian proverbs, and argues that the stone is rolled uphill, so that it returns on the roller's own head — as Wesley also reads it. Clarke matches it with a Latin tag: bad counsel is worst for its giver. Henry notes the labour, digging and rolling being work that hatred undertakes willingly, and concludes that God takes the crafty not in their craft only but in their cruelty, one plotter having hanged on his own gallows. The last verse defeats everybody. Delitzsch canvasses the versions, which read that the tongue loves not truth, and the glosses turning the sufferers into reprovers, and rejects them all because the Hebrew participle means bruised, not bruising. Gill lists four possibilities and leaves them standing. Clarke states the psychology instead: a man hates the person he has injured in proportion to the injury, and, strange to tell, to that person's innocence, as a debtor cannot bear the sight of his creditor. Henry closes with the comparison the chapter has been building toward: the slanderer proclaims war, the flatterer kisses and kills, and the second is the more dangerous.
